chunks: And Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Manqari narrated from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said:

I asked Ja'far ibn Muhammad (peace be upon him) about two groups of believers, one of which was the aggressors (bāghiyyah) and the other just ('ādilah). They fought each other, and a man from the people of Iraq killed his father, or his son, or his brother, or his close relative, while he was from the aggressors, and he was the heir of the deceased. Does he inherit him? He said, 'Yes, because he killed him with right (bi-haqq).'

key_terms.بَاغِيَةٌ: The aggressor faction (those who rebel against a just ruler or group but are not yet fully excommunicated)
key_terms.بِحَقِّ: With right/justifiably (referring to the context of factional warfare)
key_terms.عَادِلَةٌ: The just faction (those who are righteously opposing the aggressors)

ai.seo_question: Does a killer inherit from his victim if he is from the aggressor faction in a civil conflict?
ai.summary: Imam Ja'far al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that a killer from the 'aggressor' faction (bāghiyyah) retains inheritance rights from a victim of the same faction, distinguishing this from the general rule where killers are excluded. The ruling hinges on the phrase 'bi-haqq' (with right), indicating that the killing occurred within the context of legitimate factional warfare rather than a personal grievance or murder. This highlights the Shia jurisprudential nuance where the nature of the conflict determines whether the 'exclusion of the killer' rule applies.
